vignette:
Nadia is a 38-year-old woman, a mother of three, who has been married for fifteen years. She speaks softly, her hands often folded in her lap, her gaze fixed on a point just beyond my shoulder. She came to therapy at the insistence of her husband, who told her she is “not the same person anymore.”

The story she tells begins on a Tuesday afternoon, three years ago. She was working as a housekeeper for a family in a wealthy suburb. The house was large, with marble floors that reflected the light in a way she used to find beautiful. She was cleaning the master bedroom, making the bed, when the homeowner’s adult son came home unexpectedly. He was in his late twenties, someone she had seen only a few times. He seemed agitated, and she tried to make herself small, to focus on the duvet cover. He didn’t leave. He closed the door. She remembers the sound of the lock clicking. She remembers the weight of him, the smell of his cologne, the way he whispered that if she told anyone, he would say she had stolen from them. She remembers the texture of the carpet against her cheek. She does not remember leaving.

She did not call the police. She went home, took a very long shower, and told no one. She finished her shift the next day, and the day after that. She cleaned that room again, her hands trembling, her eyes on the floor. She lasted two more weeks before she quit, telling her husband the commute was too long. He was confused—she had always been so reliable—but he accepted it.

Now, she cannot step into a large, quiet room without her heart seizing. She has stopped working for any family that has an adult son living at home. She vets her clients obsessively, asking questions that feel invasive even to her, but she cannot stop. She has lost three jobs this year because she has to check every locked door in a house before she can begin cleaning. If a door is locked, she cannot touch it. She will stand in the hallway, breathing in short, shallow gasps, until she can call the homeowner and ask them to open it. She knows this looks strange. She knows they think she is unreliable or paranoid. The shame of it is a constant, dull burn in her chest.

At night, she cannot sleep. She lies next to her husband, her body rigid, listening to the house. She hears footsteps that are not there. She feels a hand on her shoulder that is not there. She has started to sleep with the lights on in the hallway, a small ritual that makes her feel foolish but terrified to abandon. Her husband has asked her why she is so jumpy. She tells him she is just tired. She cannot say the words.

The worst part, she tells me, is not the fear. It is the remembering. It comes in fragments—the click of the lock, the smell of the cologne, the weight—but not as a memory. It comes as a feeling. She will be folding laundry, and suddenly she is back on that carpet, her cheek against the fibers. She will be making a bed, and her hands will freeze, and she will have to sit down on the floor to keep from vomiting. She has started to avoid any task that involves making a bed. Her husband does it now, without comment, because he has learned that the sight of a duvet being smoothed flat makes his wife disappear into a room he cannot enter.

She is exhausted. She is ashamed. She is angry at herself for not fighting back, for not screaming, for going back to that house the next day. She carries the secret like a stone in her stomach. She has not told her husband, her mother, or her closest friend. She tells me she feels dirty, even though she has showered three times today. She tells me she is afraid she is going crazy. She is not crazy. She is trapped, right there in the middle of her own life, unable to speak the name of the room she is still locked inside.
